claims.text: The base alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, including 20 at% phosphorus.
Slow cooling of the base alloy produces multiple crystalline phases, including FCC, tetragonal, and orthorhombic phases.
Some phases formed by the base alloy are primary, phosphorus-poor phases, while other phosphide-rich phases form through eutectic or non-eutectic pathways.
Faster cooling after a short electric-arc pulse reduces the base alloy's phase population primarily to FCC A and tetragonal D.
Very rapid melt-spinning produces an amorphous structure in the base alloy.
Phosphorus enhances the glass-forming ability of the base alloy during rapid cooling.
The base alloy amorphizes only at cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
The relevant moderately rapid cooling rate is approximately 3018 K/s.
Known primary crystallization events for the base alloy occur near 960–1206 K.
The proposed intervention is to introduce approximately 2 at% boron, either by replacing part of a transition-metal constituent or by adding boron with compositional renormalization.
Boron's small atomic size and topological mismatch will increase short-range disorder and create kinetic barriers to crystalline nucleation.
Boron will interrupt regular atomic packing and reduce the thermodynamic driving force for simultaneous nucleation of multiple primary phases.
The boron-induced disorder will stabilize the undercooled liquid and reduce primary crystallization during cooling and reheating.
Approximately 2 at% boron will permit amorphous retention at cooling rates lower than those required by the undoped alloy.
Boron doping will raise the crystallization-onset temperature or significantly reduce crystallization-exotherm magnitude during reheating.
The beneficial effect should occur over cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^6 K/s.
Crystallization becomes unavoidable above approximately 960 K during reheating.
A B-containing Fe-Co-Ni-Si high-entropy alloy can form amorphous ribbons, while reduced cooling rate can produce coexisting FCC crystals and an amorphous matrix.

contradictions.description: The claimed effect extends down to roughly 10^4 K/s and the stated processing range reaches about 3018 K/s, but the proposed experiment specifies melt-spinning at only 10^5–10^6 K/s. It therefore does not directly test the predicted extension of amorphous retention into the lower cooling-rate regime.
